column1: # Probe corpus for jq evaluator error-message parity (#356).
# Each row is a filter/input pair on which the pinned jq REPORTS AN ERROR.
# ./scripts/sync-jq-error-messages.sh runs jq over every row and records the
# message it prints into tests/data/jq-error-messages.tsv, which
# tests/jq_error_message_tests.rs then asserts both succinctly evaluators
# `#` lines and blank lines are ignored. <id> must be unique and is the key
# A row on which jq does NOT error is a hard error in the sync script: this
# corpus only describes error wording, so a probe that stopped erroring is
# either a bad probe or a jq behaviour change that needs a human look.
# Group order follows the message taxonomy in
# Reaching the same sentence through `path(...)`, which used to answer with the
# path instead of refusing it (#489). Reading a path is still indexing: the
# walker asks the value evaluator, so these are the rows above wrapped.
# ── Indexing reached through paths, assignment, deletion, destructuring ──────
# `indices`/`index`/`rindex` index their input with the pattern, so a
# non-string pattern on a string input reports that same indexing error.
# … and an input they cannot search reports the same indexing error. `null`
# and an object with a string pattern are absent on purpose: jq answers those
# with `null`, so no probe can hold them (unit tests do).
# A field that isn't there reads as `null`, and `del` keeps walking the rest of
# the path against it — so an `[]` tail still raises where a `.c`/`[0]`/`[1:2]`
# Comma-group `del` routes through the multi-path walker (#424/#475); a
# non-container `.[]` sibling used to raise succinctly's own "expected array
# or object" wording instead of this sentence (#538).
# jq defines `from_entries` as object construction over the entries —
# `map({(.key // .Key // .name // .Name): …})` — so a non-string key is refused
# where it would be inserted, and `with_entries` and `{(f):v}` inherit the same
# sentence. Before #391 every entry below was silently dropped instead.
# No key alias at all, and an entry that is `null`, both leave the key `null`.
# The chain's *last* alias has nothing to be skipped in favour of, so a falsy
# `Name` is the key — `a // b` yields `b` whatever `b` is. The pair below is
# what separates that from a tail that is merely absent.
# A non-object entry is indexed with "key" all the same, so it reports the
# indexing error rather than this section's sentence.
# `with_entries` is `to_entries | map(f) | from_entries`, so an array input
# reaches `from_entries` with its indices as keys — and a filter that writes a
# The construction `from_entries` is defined over, reached directly.
# ── <v> has no keys / has no length / cannot be sorted / matched ─────────────
# `to_entries` is defined over `keys_unsorted`, so it borrows `keys`' refusal
# `<t> not a string or array` — test/match/capture's pattern argument, a
# distinct jq wording from `cannot be matched` above.
# `<v> is not a string` — scan/gsub/sub/splits's pattern argument, a
# different wording again from `not_string_or_array` just above even though
# it is the same conceptual failure (#926): jq itself uses two sentences for
# a non-string pattern depending on which builtin family raises it.
# split(re; flags) (the two-arg regex form, `Builtin::SplitRegex`) shares the
# same "<v> is not a string" wording as its scan/gsub/sub/splits siblings —
# distinct from split(sep) just below (`split_arg_non_string`), which has its
# own "split input and separator must be strings" sentence instead.
# The *flags* argument (not the pattern) to these same builtins (#928).
# test/match/capture/sub share the pattern-argument's own "<v> is not a
# string" wording. gsub/scan/split/splits instead hit an arithmetic error,
# because jq builds the internal global-flag string via concatenation
# (`flags + "g"` or `"g" + flags`) before ever checking the flags argument's
# type — operand order flips per builtin, matching the g-append-vs-prepend
# split #730 already found for *valid* flags strings.
# test/match/capture's *pattern*-argument error wording switches based on
# call arity, not the pattern's own type (#937): the bare 1-arg form uses
# `test_arg_non_string`'s "<t> not a string or array" wording above, but
# the 2-arg form (even with a valid/empty flags value) switches to the
# "<v> is not a string" wording instead — the gap the existing corpus
# missed, since it only ever probed the bare form and the flags-argument
# error separately, never a flagged call with a bad *pattern*.
# test/match/capture's *bare* form additionally unpacks a non-empty array
# pattern as [pattern, flags, ...ignored] (#943, undocumented real jq
# behavior). A genuinely empty array has no element 0 to unpack, so it
# falls through to the plain bare-form wording using the array's own type
# name; once unpacking succeeds, a bad element uses the flagged-form
# wording instead, even for a 1-element array with no explicit flags slot.
# implode's per-element error is type-specific, distinct from the whole-array
# "implode input must be an array" sentence above — see issue #706.
# Same jq definition as `ascii_downcase`, so the same sentence — probed
# because the two had drifted apart here.
# ── Errors raised inside a generator are not swallowed ───────────────────────
# ── del() through an absent container: the tail decides (#476/#527/#529) ─────
# `del(f)` is `delpaths([path(f)])`, and `path()` reads a dead end as null and
# keeps walking, so the *tail* decides whether the walk raises. A Field/Index/
# Slice tail is a no-op; an `[]` tail raises, because null refuses iteration
# even there. An out-of-range index is the only way to reach the two sites left
# The comma spelling reaches the grouped walker, the bare one the single-path
# walker; they had drifted apart (#538), so probe the comma spelling directly.
# ── path() refuses a filter that is not a path expression ────────────────────
# Distinct from the walker gaps in #483: these are expressions jq is required to
# reject by name, and `?` does not suppress the refusal (#530).
# ascii_downcase/ascii_upcase are jq prelude definitions (explode | map(...) |
# implode), so jq's own refusal fires one step deeper than the other
# pipe-to-builtin probes above -- at the exploded array's iterate step, not
# describe()/dump_truncated() rendered an overflowed/infinite float preview
# as JSON `null` instead of jq's real text. `infinite`/`-infinite`/arithmetic
# overflow have no source literal of their own, so jq shows DBL_MAX text;
# nan still has no literal spelling either way, so it stays `null` on both
# sides (unchanged, included here as a control). Uses `scan` (regex-gated,
# see FEATURE_GATED in jq_error_message_tests.rs) rather than `keys`/`.[]`,
# which route a document-sourced value through OwnedValue::to_json_for_reindex
# first - fine for a finite value, but it substitutes its own `1e999` round-
# trip sentinel for a non-finite one (#939), which is exactly what these
# probes need to NOT go through.
# ── modulemeta always errors: type-check or module-not-found (#2111) ───────
